observation_summary: Two unit tests fail because the TypedScopeCreator does not record the property 'foo' on objects created via function stubs defined inside an anonymous function, leading to missing property type information and assertion errors.
hypothesis: The original TypedScopeCreator.visit method used a custom switch that returned early for FUNCTION nodes when the parent was not a simple NAME, causing function stubs defined inside other functions to be ignored, so their type information was never attached.
prediction: The fixed version replaces the custom switch with a call to super.visit(t, n, parent), delegating to the superclass implementation that correctly processes FUNCTION, CATCH, and VAR nodes, thereby preserving type information for nested function stubs.
experiment_rationale: The diff shows the entire switch block being removed and replaced by a single super.visit call. This structural change to the method’s logic indicates an algorithmic rewrite rather than a simple guard or value change, confirming the hypothesis that the processing algorithm was flawed.
reasoning_summary: The change rewrites the core processing algorithm of TypedScopeCreator (removing a custom switch and delegating to the superclass). It is not merely adding a null/bound check, nor adjusting a constant, nor altering an API contract. Therefore the appropriate ODC type is Algorithm/Method.
evidence_used: diff replacing attachLiteralTypes + switch with super.visit
failing test assertions expecting property 'foo' to exist
bug report describing missed @param annotations for functions defined within functions

alternative_types.why_not_primary: No missing guard or condition was added; the fix changes the processing flow, not a predicate.
No constant or variable value was altered; the change is structural to the method.
Method signatures and external contracts remain unchanged.
The bug is not related to concurrency or ordering of operations.
The issue does not involve mismatched associations between separate structures.
The fix does not introduce a new capability or redesign a class; it merely corrects existing algorithmic logic.
